title: Who Is Out There: Announcements, Leases and How Long a Silence Takes to Mean Gone

questions.question: There is no registry to ask who is on the bus. How does a node know the planner is there?
options: The planner announces itself over and over and the others keep a table of who has said so lately
It asks a central registry, which every node signs in to when it starts
It looks for a subscriber on the planner's topics, which only exist while the planner runs
It sends the planner a message and waits for a reply before every use
questions.explanation: There is no registry. Each participant says it is there, repeatedly, and each of the others keeps a table of who has said so within the lease.

questions.question: A node announced at time 0 with a lease of 3 s. What does the table say at 2.9 s, 3.0 s and 3.1 s?
options: Alive at 2.9, gone at exactly 3.0, and a second gone event at 3.1
Alive at 2.9 and at exactly 3.0, and one gone event at 3.1, said once
Alive at all three: a node is only gone when it says so
Gone at 2.9 already, since no heartbeat followed the first announcement
questions.explanation: An announcement is good for the lease, up to and including its last instant. After that the table reports gone once and does not repeat it.

questions.question: What does an incarnation number tell the table?
options: How many heartbeats the node has sent, so a missed one can be counted
Which machine the node runs on, so two nodes with one name can be told apart
Each start has a new one, so a restart inside the lease can be told from a heartbeat: restarted against nothing
How long the node's lease is, so each node can choose its own
questions.explanation: A node that restarts faster than its lease never goes silent. Only a new incarnation number shows that it is not the same process that held the old state.

questions.question: The node dies and the lease is 3.5 s with a heartbeat every second. When is it noticed?
options: After one heartbeat period, 1.0 s, when the next heartbeat fails to arrive
After about one lease, 3.6 s in the test, plus the polling interval
At once, because the node's last message says it is leaving
After two leases, 7.0 s, to be sure it is not a lost heartbeat
questions.explanation: The table can only notice silence, and silence is only meaningful once it has lasted longer than the lease. So a death is seen about one lease late.

questions.question: With 10 percent of heartbeats lost, how often is a node that never dies declared gone at a lease of 1.5 s, and at 5.5 s?
options: Never at 1.5 s and 172 times at 5.5 s
17 times at both: the loss rate decides it, not the lease
Once at 1.5 s and never at 5.5 s
172 times in 2000 s at 1.5 s and never at 5.5 s
questions.explanation: At 1.5 s a single lost heartbeat crosses the lease, and one in ten is lost. At 5.5 s five in a row would have to be lost.

questions.question: What is the lease a trade between?
options: How soon a real death is noticed and how often a live node is wrongly declared gone, which the robot has to weigh
How much memory the table uses and how many nodes it can hold
How often heartbeats are sent and how large each one is
How many incarnations a node may have and how fast it may restart
questions.explanation: A short lease sees a real death quickly and cries wolf on a lossy link. A long one never cries wolf and is slow. Which cost is worse depends on the robot.
